correctness.rationale: All cases and edge conditions n>=1, 0<=K<=n and 0<a<=b<=1 are proved. When b<=1/2, t=1/2 accepts all. When a>1/2, recovery of K orientations yields the parity-improved upper bound and an adaptive alternating-orientation transcript yields the matching lower. When a<=1/2<b, finite-grid exact interval learning yields the n-K upper bound, while a three-case adversarial completion guarantees n-K rejected untouched agents and OPT=0. The endpoint case b=1 and a=1/2 is explicitly included. A standalone Fraction checker passed 140 fixed-observed minimax and 470 constructive witness comparisons; the infinitary proof does not rely on those finite tests.

originality.rationale: The exact deterministic contact-budget formula for two alternatives and public threshold intervals, including the parity correction and discontinuity at one-half, is not stated or implied without new arguments by the inspected sources. The closest primary Theorems 6.1–6.2 are restricted to at least three alternatives and rely on a third coordinate. Its general arbitrary-history bound (I.3) is not an evaluated policy minimax over limited-contact adaptive algorithms. Earlier work asks unanimous feasibility instead of minimax rejection regret. Search of published mathematical research records for threshold, two-alternative, membership-oracle, interval-stabbing and regret aliases returned no equivalent result. Full unindexed literature and the unexamined distance-loss related paper are residual risks; this is best-knowledge originality, not a guarantee.

value.rationale: The closest paper leaves two alternatives outside its deterministic lower-bound theorem because the proof uses a third alternative. Exact classification at that first missing dimension is a motivated mathematical gap. The result sharply separates always-feasible approval (b<=1/2), incompatible strict approval (a>1/2, parity benefit), and a mixed-threshold regime where the full n-K contact obstruction reappears. That boundary describes the precise robustness of a limited-elicitation social-choice process and is not merely a small numerical gain or a renaming of an existing theorem.
